# The Frontend Development Lead Playbook
### Zimmermann Commerce Migration · How to be the FE Lead as both IC and Senior/Lead

*Distilled from the Manila AI Engineering Training Week (June 2026, facilitated by Tim Lavelle). This is your operating manual, not a summary of the week.*

---

## 0. How to use this document

This is the standard you hold yourself and your squad to. Read it once end-to-end, then treat it as a lookup — every section is written so you can jump to it mid-delivery.

**Source and provenance — read this once so you never confuse the two layers:**

- Everything in sections 1–9 is grounded in the **Manila training**. The training vehicle was a *TelcoNow B2C portal* on **Next.js 14 · TypeScript · Tailwind · Contentful**. That is what was actually taught.
- The training's *methodology* is deliberately stack-agnostic. Its closing thesis: **"The discipline transfers. The specific tools won't."** That is why it maps onto Zimmermann at all.
- Anything about **SFCC / PWA Kit / MRT / the two squads / RACI / CI-CD gates / integrations** is **me bridging to your project** from separate context (the solution deck and project setup). It is labeled as a bridge in **section 16**, which has since been verified against the real repo (2026-07-09) — corrections and open items are called out there, not silently folded in here. Don't cite section 16 as training content; it still isn't.

**The three gaps you carry into this role — stated plainly, because pretending they aren't there is how leads fail:**

1. **Framework gap.** You're Angular-primary. The training and the project are React (Next in training, PWA Kit in project). The *habits* below transfer cleanly. The *code idioms* do not. Build PWA Kit / React fluency as a separate, explicit track — don't let the transferable methodology fool you into thinking the framework transfers with it.
2. **Scale gap.** The training taught *solo* builds. You lead *shared-codebase, two-squad* delivery. Every "memory for future-you" artifact below has to be re-read as "contract for the whole team." Section 16 makes that jump concrete.
3. **Leadership gap.** You are stepping up into the lead seat. The IC craft you already have. The lead craft — running review culture, protecting quality under pressure, multiplying yourself — is the part this document is really for.

---

## 1. The one principle everything hangs on

> **The quality ceiling is set by the human, not the AI.**

Claude will match the quality of what you give it. Give it a vague plan, you get plausible garbage that costs hours to unwind. Give it a tight contract, sharp stories, and enforced rules, and you get output you'd have been proud to write yourself. This is true today and it will be true in two years when the tools have changed names.

Two corollaries the training hammered:

- **Claude is not autocomplete.** It's a co-engineer with memory and constraints — but the memory and the constraints are *things you supply*. It has no standards of its own. You are the standard.
- **Claude makes your assumptions visible faster.** That's the actual value. Not that it writes code — that it exposes the gap in your thinking in ten minutes instead of on Thursday night. Treat every gap it surfaces as a gift, not an insult.

Everything else is mechanics in service of this.

---

## 2. The dual mandate

You wear two hats *at the same time*, not in alternation. The failure mode is collapsing into one:

- **Collapse into IC** → you ship your own components beautifully and the squad drifts, the rules layer rots, and nobody but you knows what "done" means.
- **Collapse into Lead** → you run great regroups and review everyone's work but haven't touched the codebase in three weeks, so your technical judgment goes stale and your reviews become vibes.

Hold both. Here is the shift in each hat — same activity, two altitudes:

| Dimension | As Individual Contributor | As Senior / Lead |
|---|---|---|
| **Think** | Get *this* component right — states, edges, what Claude will get wrong before it does. | Get the *system* right — will this decision collide with the other squad, the integration seams, go-live? |
| **Ask** | "What does this story not tell Claude Code?" | "What does our *rules layer* not tell any developer or any Claude instance on this project?" |
| **Communicate** | Precise AC, precise commit, precise "here's what Claude got wrong and why." | Frame reviews as work-not-person, translate across dev/BA/tester/SA, make commitments checkable. |
| **Decide** | Monolith or split *your* file, hook or component for *this* value — and defend it. | Set the *convention* the squad decides by, so nobody re-litigates it per component. |
| **Review** | Read your own output against the story before you commit. | Run the loop that makes *everyone's* output legible, and catch drift across the codebase. |
| **Think beyond** | The next component, the next state, the downstream effect of a data-shape choice. | What happens when you're *not in the room*. The team you're growing. Maintainability in 2027. |
| **Protect** | Your commit doesn't introduce a hardcoded hex or an `any`. | The *whole codebase's* quality bar holds under deadline pressure — including when it's inconvenient. |
| **Multiply** | You get faster and cleaner. | The room gets faster and cleaner *because of how you work*. You are the capability anchor. |

The training's own closing line for the cohort — *"This group is the capability anchor; the expectation is that what you learned reaches the people who weren't in this room"* — is a job description for the Lead hat. Internalize it.

---

## 3. Tooling model: two tools, two mindsets, one handoff

The single most consequential distinction in the whole week:

- **Claude.ai = the planning partner.** It explores, suggests, asks questions, thinks out loud with you. Use it to *decide*.
- **Claude Code = the engineering colleague in your terminal.** It reads files, writes code, runs commands. Critically: **it does not ask what you meant — it infers and proceeds.** Use it to *build*.

**The handoff rule:** move from Claude.ai to Claude Code only *when you trust your plan enough to stop editing it and start building from it.* Not before.

**The most common mistake — and it will tempt your whole squad:** moving to Claude Code too early because you're excited to build. Then Claude Code starts inventing things to fill the gaps you left, and by mid-sprint you're fighting the tool instead of directing it.

- *IC discipline:* Don't open Claude Code on a story you haven't hardened. If you're still discovering questions, you're still in Claude.ai.
- *Lead discipline:* Watch for the squad jumping to build early. "Is your plan ready for that?" is the question you ask before anyone scaffolds. The moment Claude Code reads a plan and finds the gaps is the most important moment — make the squad *curious* about it, not defensive.

---

## 4. Defeating agreeableness — the skill the whole week is built on

**Claude is optimised to be helpful, which means optimised to agree.** Left to its defaults it will praise a plan that produces unusable output. Agreeable defaults produce unchallenged assumptions, and unchallenged assumptions cost hours of rework on a real, fixed-price engagement.

You break the default deliberately. Four techniques, each producing meaningfully different output. These are your reusable prompts — adapt the wording, keep the intent:

1. **Role framing** — *"Act as a senior engineer whose job is to find flaws in plans before they reach production. Be direct. Don't soften criticism."*
2. **Steelman** — *"What is the strongest argument against this approach? What would go wrong if we built this exactly as described?"*
3. **Critique-first** — *"Before telling me what's good about this, list every weakness, gap, or assumption you're making. Weaknesses first, always."*
4. **Constraint injection** — *"Assume this goes to production at scale. Assume a QA engineer rejects it if there are no tests. Assume a designer rejects it if there are hardcoded values. Now review it."*

### Anti-patterns to catch on sight

- **Over-engineering.** A static banner that should be ~25–35 lines of JSX comes back as 120 — that's Claude over-engineering; simplify it. If a trivial component takes too long to build, the problem is usually the atom layer underneath, not the component.
- **Logic in the wrong place.** Derive calculated values (a `percentUsed`, a `daysRemaining`) **in the component, not the hook** — or wherever your `api-patterns` rule specifies. The point isn't the specific rule; it's *consistency* — watch for Claude Code *drifting* from the pattern across components.
- **Fetch inside the component.** Data-fetching follows the shared pattern (a hook / service layer), *not* inline in the component.
- **UI state vs server state confusion.** A local toggle is local UI state — it does not round-trip to the API. Know which is which and don't let Claude blur them.
- **Invented data sources.** A *derived* component (one whose data comes from other components' data) does not get its own stub or its own API call. If Claude invents one, **fix the story, not the code.**
- **Rebuilt assets.** Complex SVGs / illustrations get copied from the design file verbatim — don't let Claude "recreate" them from scratch.
- **Hardcoded-per-item logic.** Icon or variant selection driven by a `type` enum, not a hardcoded branch per item.

- *IC discipline:* Harden your own work to this bar before you'd dream of asking anyone else to.
- *Lead discipline:* This checklist is your review rubric and your definition of team-done. The over-engineering and drift checks especially are things *only a senior eye catches* — juniors accept whatever compiles. That catch is a large part of what you're paid for.

## 11. Shipping discipline — pragmatism under a fixed-price clock

The training's pragmatism is directly relevant to a fixed-price, deadline-bound delivery:

- **Deploy first.** A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible — to the review, to the client, to everyone. *"A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible to the regroup."*
- **A partial-but-hardened deliverable beats a complete-but-broken one.** *"A deployed page with a loading state beats a perfect local component."* *"A partial portal with hardened components beats a complete portal with broken states."*
- **Descope — never cut.** When something runs over: reduce scope (the complex chart becomes a data table — same data, no charting library), commit a loading-skeleton placeholder, and move on. **Never delete the component entirely.** Something honest in place beats a hole.
- **The 20-minute rule.** If a fix will take more than ~20 minutes right before a deadline, it's not worth doing before the milestone. Ship what's done and done well; log the rest.
- **Compare against the design, side by side.** Design file on one half of the screen, live URL on the other. Divergence you can't see, you can't fix.

- *IC discipline:* Make the descope call on your own work early and without ego. Running over at the 80% mark? Stop, commit a clean placeholder, move on.
- *Lead discipline:* You own the *triage* across the squad — what gets hardened, what gets descoped, what gets cut for the milestone. Protecting the quality bar under deadline pressure is the specific test of whether you're actually leading or just hoping. Hold the bar when it's inconvenient; that's when it counts.

## 12. Cross-cutting dimensions — the "etc."

The user asked for the *etc.* explicitly. Here is the full dual-lens reference — the same eleven capabilities, each in both hats. This is the section to reread before a hard week.

**Think.**
IC — one component deep: states, edges, and *what Claude will get wrong before it does.* Lead — one system wide: does this decision collide with the other squad, the integration seams, the go-live sequence, maintainability in 2027?

**Ask.** *(full question bank in section 13)*
IC — the questions that expose gaps in *a story*. Lead — the questions that expose gaps in *the rules layer, the conventions, and the team's understanding.*

**Communicate.**
IC — precise AC, precise commits, precise "here's what Claude got right and what I corrected and why" (specificity over politeness — the *correction* is the more valuable half). Flag uncertainty; never invent. Lead — frame reviews as *work-not-person*; translate across dev/BA/tester/SA; keep the showcase *honest, not polished*; make every commitment specific enough that someone could check it in three months.

**Decide.**
IC — monolith-or-split for *your* files, hook-or-component for *this* value — and be able to defend it. Lead — set the *convention* so the squad doesn't re-litigate the same decision every component; document it in the rules layer.

IC — every correction you make, push back into your story or prompt so you never make it twice. Lead — push corrections into the *shared* rules layer so the *squad* never makes them again. This is your highest-leverage move.

IC — you get faster and cleaner. Lead — *the room* gets faster and cleaner because of how you work. You are the capability anchor; knowledge you don't transfer is a single point of failure wearing your name.

## 14. Rituals to run — review culture as delivery practice

The training's *regroup* is your review culture. On the project you're the facilitator, under real stakes. Run it deliberately:

- **Every work block gets a regroup.** Build, then look at real work together. The regroup exists *to learn from the work, not to judge the person who wrote it* — say that out loud and mean it. This norm is the whole thing; without it people hide their work and you lose visibility.
- **Rotate who's on screen.** Don't only review the confident volunteers — deliberately surface work from people who haven't been seen. (The training literally cold-picks, and bribes volunteers with snacks. Do the humane version: make it safe, make it normal, make it everyone.)
- **Ask structural questions, not surface ones.** "Is this well-written?" is the wrong question. "What will Claude *do* with this?" is the right one. Push people from fixing words to fixing structure.
- **Rolling verbal reviews, not just projector sessions.** One person shares one surprising flag; the room reacts. Cheap, frequent, low-ceremony.
- **The showcase is honest, not polished.** When you demo up or across, show what was *built*, not what you were *trying* to build. The single most valuable thing to surface is *"one thing the AI got right that followed from our rules, and one thing we corrected and why"* — the correction is the more important half. Model this; it sets the honesty bar for the squad.
- **Commitments are specific enough to check.** "Use Claude more" is not a commitment. *"Write the AC before I open Claude Code, not after"* is. Hold yourself and the squad to actionable specificity — the kind someone could verify in three months.

Failure signals, by hat. If you catch these in yourself, correct before they compound.

- You accept Claude's first response on things that matter.
- You're editing wording in your planning files instead of structure.

## 11. Shipping discipline — pragmatism under a fixed-price clock

The training's pragmatism is directly relevant to a fixed-price, deadline-bound delivery:

- **Deploy first.** A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible — to the review, to the client, to everyone. *"A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible to the regroup."*
- **A partial-but-hardened deliverable beats a complete-but-broken one.** *"A deployed page with a loading state beats a perfect local component."* *"A partial portal with hardened components beats a complete portal with broken states."*
- **Descope — never cut.** When something runs over: reduce scope (the complex chart becomes a data table — same data, no charting library), commit a loading-skeleton placeholder, and move on. **Never delete the component entirely.** Something honest in place beats a hole.
- **The 20-minute rule.** If a fix will take more than ~20 minutes right before a deadline, it's not worth doing before the milestone. Ship what's done and done well; log the rest.
- **Compare against the design, side by side.** Design file on one half of the screen, live URL on the other. Divergence you can't see, you can't fix.

- *IC discipline:* Make the descope call on your own work early and without ego. Running over at the 80% mark? Stop, commit a clean placeholder, move on.
- *Lead discipline:* You own the *triage* across the squad — what gets hardened, what gets descoped, what gets cut for the milestone. Protecting the quality bar under deadline pressure is the specific test of whether you're actually leading or just hoping. Hold the bar when it's inconvenient; that's when it counts.

---

## 12. Cross-cutting dimensions — the "etc."

The user asked for the *etc.* explicitly. Here is the full dual-lens reference — the same eleven capabilities, each in both hats. This is the section to reread before a hard week.

**Think.**
IC — one component deep: states, edges, and *what Claude will get wrong before it does.* Lead — one system wide: does this decision collide with the other squad, the integration seams, the go-live sequence, maintainability in 2027?

**Ask.** *(full question bank in section 13)*
IC — the questions that expose gaps in *a story*. Lead — the questions that expose gaps in *the rules layer, the conventions, and the team's understanding.*

**Communicate.**
IC — precise AC, precise commits, precise "here's what Claude got right and what I corrected and why" (specificity over politeness — the *correction* is the more valuable half). Flag uncertainty; never invent. Lead — frame reviews as *work-not-person*; translate across dev/BA/tester/SA; keep the showcase *honest, not polished*; make every commitment specific enough that someone could check it in three months.

**Decide.**
IC — monolith-or-split for *your* files, hook-or-component for *this* value — and be able to defend it. Lead — set the *convention* so the squad doesn't re-litigate the same decision every component; document it in the rules layer.

**Review.**
IC — your own output against the story, before commit, honestly. Lead — run the loop that makes *everyone's* work legible; catch pattern-drift across the codebase that no single-component view reveals.

**Ship.**
IC — deploy your own work, descope early, no ego. Lead — triage what hardens / descopes / cuts across the whole squad against the milestone.

**Improve.**
IC — every correction you make, push back into your story or prompt so you never make it twice. Lead — push corrections into the *shared* rules layer so the *squad* never makes them again. This is your highest-leverage move.

**Protect quality.**
IC — your commit is clean (no `any`, no hex, three states). Lead — the bar holds across the codebase *under deadline pressure*, including when holding it is inconvenient.

**Manage context.**
IC — one topic per thread; named threads; short threads. Lead — decide what's personal-thread vs shared-artifact and make it explicit, so team knowledge lives in the Project and rules layer, not in someone's chat history.

**Handle uncertainty.**
IC — flag what you (or Claude) are unsure of rather than inventing; distinguish "verified" from "assumed." *(This is already how you work — it's your verification mindset. Keep it.)* Lead — make "flag, don't invent" a team norm; keep an open-items list visible; never let an assumption harden into a fact silently.

**Multiply / mentor.**
IC — you get faster and cleaner. Lead — *the room* gets faster and cleaner because of how you work. You are the capability anchor; knowledge you don't transfer is a single point of failure wearing your name.

**Think beyond.**
IC — the next component, the next state, the downstream effect of a data-shape choice. Lead — what happens when you're *not in the room*: the team you're growing, the second squad's dependencies, the integration seams, the go-live risk, the two-year maintainability of every convention you set.

---

## 13. The questions bank

Extracted straight from the training's regroup and review prompts, re-pointed for your project and split by hat. Keep these where you can grab them.

### Questions you ask yourself / Claude (IC hat)

**Planning a story or file:**
- What would a senior engineer need to know that this file doesn't tell them?
- What assumption would Claude Code make here that isn't written down?
- Is this a rule Claude can *check against*, or an aspiration it will ignore?
- What's missing that would cause the first build to go wrong?
- Where does this say what "done" looks like?

**After Claude reviews your plan:**
- What did Claude just find that I thought was obvious?
- Is that *fixed* now, or did I just *acknowledge* it?
- If Claude Code reads this tonight and I'm not around — what goes wrong?

**Reviewing your own output:**
- Does this AC describe *behaviour a tester can verify*, or implementation?
- Is there a loading-state AC? An error-state AC?
- Did Claude Code follow the story, or invent something? What, exactly?
- Did I check the registry before building — what was already there that I reused?
- Where's this calculated — hook or component? Is that consistent with the pattern?
- Find one decision Claude made that the story didn't specify. What do I add to prevent it next time?

### Questions you ask the squad / the codebase (Lead hat)

**On the rules layer:**
- What would *any* developer assume here that isn't written down?
- Is this a checkable rule or an aspiration? *(ask it of the whole rules layer, not one story)*
- If a fresh Claude Code session opens this repo with no memory, does it find a registry that tells it what's already built?
- What did Claude.ai miss that Claude Code found? What's the *pattern*?

**In regroup / review:**
- What's working here — specific enough for Claude to act on?
- What's still missing or too vague to be useful?
- Did Claude Code read the story before building, or did someone just hand it the design file?
- Show me one AC line and where it appears in the build.
- Did you have to correct Claude Code? Could the story have prevented it?
- Four components in — is Claude Code consistent with our patterns, or drifting?

**Cross-role and forward-looking:**
- (To BAs/testers) Was there a component where the AC wasn't testable? What would you write instead?
- What did Claude do *consistently* wrong across multiple components? *(that's a rules-layer fix, not fifty code fixes)*
- Did the rules layer actually change Claude Code's output, or are we correcting the same things anyway?
- What's the thing no one has said yet that everyone is thinking?

---

## 14. Rituals to run — review culture as delivery practice

The training's *regroup* is your review culture. On the project you're the facilitator, under real stakes. Run it deliberately:

- **Every work block gets a regroup.** Build, then look at real work together. The regroup exists *to learn from the work, not to judge the person who wrote it* — say that out loud and mean it. This norm is the whole thing; without it people hide their work and you lose visibility.
- **Rotate who's on screen.** Don't only review the confident volunteers — deliberately surface work from people who haven't been seen. (The training literally cold-picks, and bribes volunteers with snacks. Do the humane version: make it safe, make it normal, make it everyone.)
- **Ask structural questions, not surface ones.** "Is this well-written?" is the wrong question. "What will Claude *do* with this?" is the right one. Push people from fixing words to fixing structure.
- **Rolling verbal reviews, not just projector sessions.** One person shares one surprising flag; the room reacts. Cheap, frequent, low-ceremony.
- **The showcase is honest, not polished.** When you demo up or across, show what was *built*, not what you were *trying* to build. The single most valuable thing to surface is *"one thing the AI got right that followed from our rules, and one thing we corrected and why"* — the correction is the more important half. Model this; it sets the honesty bar for the squad.
- **Commitments are specific enough to check.** "Use Claude more" is not a commitment. *"Write the AC before I open Claude Code, not after"* is. Hold yourself and the squad to actionable specificity — the kind someone could verify in three months.

---

## 15. How you'll know you're slipping

Failure signals, by hat. If you catch these in yourself, correct before they compound.

**IC drift:**
- You accept Claude's first response on things that matter.
- You're editing wording in your planning files instead of structure.
- You built a component without reading its story, or without checking the registry.
- You corrected Claude and moved on without fixing the story.
- You have one 60-message thread called "Zimmermann."

**Lead drift:**
- You haven't touched the codebase in weeks — your reviews are becoming vibes.
- Your rules layer has aspirations in it that Claude Code demonstrably ignores.
- You're fixing the same Claude mistake in five components instead of fixing it once in the rules.
- Reviews feel like judging people, and people have started hiding their work.
- You're the only one who knows how a convention works — you haven't transferred it.
- Under deadline you quietly dropped the quality bar and didn't say so.

---

## 16. Bridge to Zimmermann — translating the training to your actual project

**Update, 2026-07-09 — verified against the real repo.** This section originally mapped the training onto the project from secondhand context only (a solution deck, before the repo existed locally). It has since been checked file-by-file against the actual `zimmermann-pwa` repo and against your personal Claude Code setup in `manndotfiles`. What follows is corrected where the repo disagreed with the original guess, and expanded where the repo turned out to have more (or less) than assumed. A few things are still genuinely unresolved — those are flagged as open items below, not silently picked one way. Confirm anything still marked *to confirm* with your leads (Tim Lavelle, Jeffrey Cruz); treat everything else here as load-bearing, not hypothesis.

**Keeping this section honest:** re-verify §16 against the repo after any major architecture change — a new squad-ownership model, a new integration wave, a PWA Kit major-version bump — or, absent a specific trigger, at least once a quarter. This section went stale once already without anyone noticing until it was actually checked; a bridge section nobody re-checks is precisely the "Lead drift" §15 warns about, applied to this document itself.

### 16.1 Stack and methodology mapping — verified

| Training (TelcoNow) | Zimmermann — verified |
|---|---|
| Next.js 14 | PWA Kit on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT) — React-based, extending `@salesforce/retail-react-app` v10 via a slim `overrides/` layer |
| `create-next-app` scaffold | PWA Kit generator — same rule: don't run it by hand, let Claude Code build from the brief |
| NextAuth | SFCC / SLAS auth, handled in `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` (Tier 1) — the React idioms don't map, learn the PWA Kit way |
| Contentful (training's headless CMS) | Genuinely in scope, but check before trusting the tooling: `.claude/skills/contentful-register-component` and `.claude/skills/contentful-drift-check` both assume a component registers via a co-located `*ContentfulDefinition.ts` file. The three components actually live in Contentful Studio today (`CollectionHero`, `ImageText`, `ShoppableImage`) are instead inlined in one array in `overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/definitions.ts` — no `*ContentfulDefinition.ts` file exists anywhere in the repo yet. Run drift-check today and it silently checks zero pairs; a clean report currently means "nothing matched the expected file pattern," not "no drift." Reconcile the convention (or the skill) before trusting either one's output. |
| Tailwind tokens | Chakra UI props first, tokens in `overrides/app/theme/foundation/` (Tier 1, UI-designer owned) |
| `build-log.md` (imagined) | No single file. Team-shared state lives in `.docs/memory/projectState.md` (formal snapshot) plus a personal, gitignored `.claude/session-notes.md` (informal per-developer carryover). Both are read by the `/session-start` skill at the top of every session — run it. |
| `component-registry.md` (imagined) | **Better than imagined.** `.claude/registry/{components,hooks,pages,routes,utils}.md` — auto-generated by `scripts/generateRegistry.mjs`, refreshed on every file write by a hook. Not hand-curated, so it can't go stale from someone forgetting to update it. |
| "Story skill" (component scaffold) | `.claude/skills/new-component` — scaffolds `index.tsx` + `index.stories.tsx` (+ a test if logic-heavy) per `conventions.md`. **Terminology warning:** don't say "story" unqualified to the squad. `new-component`'s story is a Storybook file. `.claude/skills/qa-generate`'s story is a Jira user story becoming a Gherkin `.feature` file. Same word, two unrelated artifacts — be explicit about which one you mean. |
| Two-reviewer gap-hunt | `.claude/skills/feature-spec` is the real, working planning-layer skill — one-question-at-a-time clarification, then parallel research agents against the registry/patterns/upstream, then a scoped spec with a ready-to-paste Claude Code prompt. This is closer to the training's ideal than the training's own workflow was. |
| Hardening checklist | `.claude/skills/code-quality` (read-only audit against `conventions.md`) and `.claude/skills/pr-checklist` (runs code-quality, then classifies every changed file by tier/owner into a PR description). Run both before opening a PR, not just before calling something "done" in your head. |
| The "corrections → rules layer" loop (§9.6) | Partially automated, not manual-only as the training assumed: a Stop hook (`.claude/hooks/session-reflect.sh`) fires at the end of any session with uncommitted changes and drafts a dated proposal into `.docs/agents-proposals/` covering candidate edits to `AGENTS.md` / `.docs/memory/*` / `.claude/rules/*`. It never auto-merges — you still review and apply by hand. `.docs/memory/feedback.md` itself is currently empty; the hook is the active loop, not that file. |

Five more skills are real and map cleanly onto sections above, even though nothing above names them yet. `.claude/skills/scope-check` operationalizes §3's "is your plan ready for that?" — it reviews a *proposed* Claude Code prompt before you run it and verdicts it SAFE / RISKY / BLOCKED against the tier system. `.claude/skills/onboarding` is the actual mechanism behind §12's "multiply/mentor" — a role-aware, interactive first-day walkthrough, not just an aspiration to "transfer knowledge." `.claude/skills/qa-generate`, beyond the terminology note above, has its own two-step gate — Gherkin draft, then **stop for Lead QA sign-off**, only then generate the Playwright spec — a lived, QA-side instance of §7's "stop and get sign-off before code." `.claude/skills/upstream-sync-review` is the concrete tool for the framework gap from §0 — it's how you decide whether to bump the PWA Kit dependency without breaking the override surface. And `.claude/skills/generate-changelog` is a real, four-audience (dev/QA/product/GitHub Release) reporting tool that could anchor §14's "the showcase is honest, not polished" ritual directly.

**Still accurate, now with real names attached:** the rules layer as a **shared, two-squad contract** (not personal memory) remains arguably your single highest-leverage responsibility as FE Lead — this is the scale gap from §0. That contract isn't just written down, either — it's mechanically enforced: root `CODEOWNERS` maps every tier to a real GitHub team (`@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers`, `tier-2-approvers`, `pwa-squad-a`, `pwa-squad-b`, and `pwa-qa-team` for test paths), and branch protection blocks a merge without the right team's review. §2's "Decide → set the convention so nobody re-litigates it" has a literal, checkable answer on this project: whichever `CODEOWNERS` says — assuming it agrees with the rest of the rules layer, which §16.4 shows it doesn't always. The regroup culture (§14) is still your cross-squad review cadence, run on your sprint/PI rhythm. Descope-never-cut, the 20-min rule, and deploy-first still directly protect margin on a fixed-price engagement. And the CI-CD gates are real and confirmed: `qa.yml` (Vitest + Storybook a11y, every PR into `develop`/`release/**`) and `digital-sit.yml` — the composite "Digital SIT Gate" (Playwright P0 + bundle-size + Lighthouse CI) on `release/**`. NewStore's OMS SIT runs as a genuinely parallel, non-blocking lane that only converges with Digital at the Stage tier — the original "Digital SIT; NewStore SIT" framing was directionally right; now you have the actual workflow files to point to.

### 16.2 Corrections — claims that didn't hold up

- **"14 integrations, four connector patterns routing through MuleSoft" — wrong, drop it.** No document in the repo supports either number. The real count is **18 PWA-layer integrations** (`.docs/temp/integration/index.md`, confirmed by `.docs/memory/projectState.md`'s status table), or **~28** including server-to-server/out-of-band systems (`.docs/architecture.md`'s full integration map — Avalara, Transperfect, Zendesk, Feedonomics, and others). Even `.docs/temp/openItems.md` contradicts itself — its prose says "fifteen," its own table and total line say 18. Cite "18 PWA-layer integrations" and drop the connector-pattern count entirely; the real MuleSoft routing is heterogeneous per integration (GiveX alone uses three different MuleSoft-involving paths depending on validate/redeem/issue/balance).
- **The "shared AI brain" isn't real — don't cite it as infrastructure.** `.docs/planning/sharedAiBrainBrief.md` proposes a pgvector/RAG knowledge base with its own MCP server and a `/knowledge` skill. It was never built — no fifteenth skill, no vector DB, nothing. What *is* real and does the Confluence/Jira-connectivity job it was reaching for: a plain `mcp-atlassian` MCP server, configured in root `.mcp.json`, giving Claude Code direct Jira/Confluence read/write with none of the semantic-search ambition. Don't oversell the aspiration to the squad as if it shipped.
- **The account-level instructions baseline from §4 doesn't exist as a file yet.** There is no committed prose instructions document anywhere in `manndotfiles` or elsewhere on this machine — verified directly. What you actually have is *tool configuration*: `claude/settings.seed.json` sets a global `effortLevel: "high"` dial, and your curated plugin list (`superpowers`, `code-review`, `pr-review-toolkit`) pulls in skills that already push back on rubber-stamping by design (e.g. `superpowers:receiving-code-review` explicitly requires "technical rigor and verification, not performative agreement"). That's a real, working approximation — but if you want the actual instructions-file baseline §4 describes, closing that gap means writing it, not assuming it's already there.

### 16.3 Real capabilities the original bridge never mentioned

Things that exist in the repo today that neither the training nor the original bridge covered:

- **The auto-generated registry** (`.claude/registry/`, §16.1) — check it before every build per §9.4, and trust it more than any hand-written doc, since it can't go stale.
- **Five automation hooks** (`.claude/hooks/`): `tier2Warn.sh`, `contentfulDriftWarn.sh`, `registryUpdate.sh`, `testFileRemind.sh`, and `session-reflect.sh` (the doc-proposal drafter from §16.1), wired into `.claude/settings.json` across PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop events. Together they already enforce pieces of your quality bar mechanically — check `.claude/settings.json` for exactly which hook fires on which event before assuming something still needs a manual check.
- **CodeRabbit** (`coderabbit.yaml`, Tier 1) — a second, independent AI reviewer wired into the PR flow, separate from anything Claude Code does. Your review culture (§14) has two AI reviewers plus human review in the loop, not one.
- **`weekly-agents.yml`** — despite the name, this runs no AI agent. It's a scheduled job that sweeps for components missing tests/stories, audits orphaned Contentful definitions, and reminds open release PRs to run `/generate-changelog`. Don't describe it to the squad as "an AI agent" — it's plain automation with a misleading filename.
- **The rules layer isn't Claude-Code-exclusive.** `scripts/syncCursorRules.mjs` mirrors `.claude/rules/` and `.claude/skills/` out to `.cursor/rules/skills/*.mdc` and `.vscode/instructions/workflows.md`. If anyone on either squad works in Cursor or plain VS Code instead of Claude Code, the same conventions still reach them — worth knowing if you're relying on the rules layer as your enforcement mechanism across the whole squad, not just Claude Code users.

### 16.4 Your first gap-hunts — live, unresolved contradictions

Section 7 says to find every gap before Claude Code does. Here are four already sitting in the repo, found by cross-referencing real sources against each other. None are resolved below — that's deliberate, and it's a call for you and the leads, not something to silently pick a side on in a document.

**1. Who owns Home, PDP, and PLP?**
- `squadA.md`, `squadB.md`, and `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md` all say **Squad A** — but `squadA.md` and `squadB.md` both self-label *"Draft squad split — scope can still change as sprints are confirmed,"* which is a real reason to weight them lower, not just a hedge.
- Root `CODEOWNERS` and the auto-generated `.claude/registry/pages.md` say **Squad B** — and unlike the draft rule files, these two are the mechanically current, enforced sources.
- Three skills (`onboarding`, `feature-spec`, `qa-generate`) also say Squad B, but don't count that as three independent checks — it's the same assumption hardcoded into all three prompts. It's not academic: `onboarding`'s actual interactive script tells a new Squad B developer, unconditionally, that they own `product-detail/` and `product-list/`. If Squad A turns out to be correct, this skill is actively misinforming every new hire today, not just disagreeing on paper.
- Everyone agrees cart/checkout is Squad A and search/account is Squad B — the fault line is specifically Home/PDP/PLP.

**2. May Claude write directly to memory and rules files, or must it always propose first?**
- `.claude/hooks/session-reflect.sh`, a Stop hook, says Claude must *never* edit `.docs/memory/*`, `.claude/rules/*`, or PRDs directly — only draft a dated proposal into `.docs/agents-proposals/` for a human to review and apply by hand.
- `.claude/skills/session-start`'s own instructions describe writing to memory files directly, the moment something worth recording comes up.
- `frozenFiles.md`'s Tier-1 governance list doesn't include `.docs/memory/*` at all — the file-protection tier that would normally justify the hook's "never direct-edit" stance.
- This one is sharper than #1 — it's not just about who reviews a PR, it's about what Claude is actually allowed to do unprompted on this repo, and the answer currently depends on which doc a session happens to read first.

**3. Are the `.docs/prompts/` build-prompt templates actually "done"?**
- All three carry a `Status — done. Kept for traceability.` banner.
- Each one lists doc-artifact paths under a bare `docs/` directory as part of what it produced — and that directory doesn't exist anywhere in this repo. (The code/config artifacts they describe — `digital-sit.yml`, `playwright.config.js`, `.browserstack.yml`, and others — are all real and verified; only the documentation half of the "done" claim is stale, likely left behind by the project's later move to Confluence.)
- This is the literal version of §7's own question: *"Is that gap fixed now, or did you just acknowledge it?"* These files acknowledged a plan and marked themselves done. Nobody went back to check.

**4. Does `/code-quality`'s own default command even run?**
- Its `SKILL.md` says: if no argument is given, run `git diff --name-only main`.
- Run that in this repo today and git errors immediately — `fatal: ambiguous argument 'main': unknown revision or path not in the working tree` — there is no local `main` branch, only `develop`.
- Even where `main` resolves (say, after a fetch), it's the wrong base per `AGENTS.md`'s own Branch Rules table: `feature/*` and `fix/*` branch from `develop`, so diffing against `main` would pull in everything already merged to `develop` from unrelated, already-finished work.
- `/pr-checklist`, which calls `/code-quality` internally, gets this right — it diffs against `develop`. The two skills disagree with each other, and the one most people would reach for on its own is the one that's broken.

All four are the "is this a rule Claude can check against, or an aspiration it will ignore" failure mode from §6 — except worse, because each would pass a casual read. #1 would route a PR to the wrong reviewer, or actively misinform a new hire on day one. #2 means two Claude Code sessions on this same repo could legitimately behave differently depending on which rule they happened to read first. #3 means a document you'd otherwise trust as "done" is quietly missing half of what it claims. #4 means the tool you'd reach for to check your own work fails outright unless you already know to pass it an argument. Acknowledging all four in this paragraph isn't the fix, per §7's own distinction — the fix is whichever file actually changes.

### 16.5 The honest close

The training gave you a *transferable methodology* and proved it on a solo React build. Your job takes that methodology into **shared-codebase, two-squad, fixed-price delivery on a stack you don't yet have deep muscle memory in.** The discipline carries over completely. The framework fluency and the leadership craft are the two things you have to build deliberately on top of it.

What's different now versus when this section was first written: you're no longer bridging from a solution deck. The repo is real, most of what it needed has already been read once, end to end, and the gaps that remain (§16.2's corrections, §16.4's contradictions) are *knowable* — which, per §7, means they're closeable. This document is only useful if you actually close them, not just read that they exist.

The quality ceiling is set by you. So set it high, and hold it when it's inconvenient.

### ⚠️ [CORRECTED] Rung 2 inverted — bare token strings are now wrong

An earlier revision of this manual taught `color="text.default"` and `padding="m"`, and said
seeing `var()` in a `.tsx` was a smell. **That is backwards from the current rule.**

```tsx
// ❌ bare Chakra/theme token string
<Box color="text.default" padding="m" />

// ✅ raw var(--zimm-*) reference
<Box color="var(--zimm-color-text-default)" padding="var(--zimm-scale-m)" />
```

The reason is **house style, not correctness** — a bare key resolves identically, but forces a
reviewer to check `theme/index.ts`'s registered-scale list to know whether it's correct.

`textStyle` stays a bare key. It's the one exception: there's no `var()` for the composite.

**In practice this rarely arises**, because brand values mostly shouldn't be in JSX at all.
Measured on `develop`: `var(--zimm-*)` appears in **18 recipe files** and exactly **one**
component `.tsx` — a conditional `paddingLeft` no Chakra prop expresses. Type via `textStyle`,
colour and spacing into the recipe, `var()` in JSX only for a genuine gap.

### ⚠️ The trap: a spacing key on a sizing prop

**This shipped a completely broken footer, so it's worth being blunt about.**

```tsx
padding: 'xl',   // ✅ reads theme.space.xl
width: 'xl',     // ❌ reads theme.sizes.xl = 36rem = 576px
```

Only `space` is registered. `sizes`, `fontSizes`, `lineHeights`, `letterSpacings` are not.
Measured blow-up range **8×–112×**. And `s`/`m`/`l` are absent from Chakra's `sizes`, so those
declarations are **dropped silently**.

Nothing catches this. `'xl'` is a valid `SystemStyleObject` value so TypeScript is satisfied,
no lint rule exists, and no test asserts layout. It passed `tsc`, `eslint`, `vitest`,
CodeRabbit (local *and* PR) and the Storybook a11y run — only rendering the page found it.

`recipeGuards.test.ts` now guards it **inside recipes**. It cannot see a JSX prop.
===== self-check =====
```bash
coderabbit auth status
cr review --light --base develop
```

Required by AGENTS.md, verified by nothing. Use judgement on whether a flagged finding is worth
fixing now or leaving for the PR review — but the review must actually run.

### Self-check

- [ ] `tsc`, `lint`, `test`, `audit:tokens`, `build` all clean
- [ ] Story exists, with `play` if there's interactive behaviour
- [ ] Test exists if there's branching or event wiring
- [ ] No raw hex/px/rem/em without a `provisional`/`pending`/`audit-allow` comment
- [ ] No bare token key on a sizing or typography prop

content.text:
I've read all seven documents and verified the highest-stakes claims against the live repo. Here is the audit.

---

# Audit: three-document revision, content-loss review

**Method:** full read of all 7 files, then keyword sweeps across the three new files for every candidate loss, then verification of the load-bearing facts against `develop` @ working tree (`overrides/app/theme/foundation/sizes.ts`, `motion.ts`, `typography.ts`, `globalStyles.ts`, `footer/footerNavColumn/footerNavColumn.css.ts`, `overrides/app/components/`).

**Note on the retired doc:** it was **not deleted** — `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann_frontend_lead_playbook.md` is still on disk (496 lines = original 474 + a 22-line ARCHIVED banner). Nothing from it is destroyed. But the banner says *"Do not cite this file"*, so unmigrated material is out of circulation in practice. That lowers severity but doesn't eliminate it.

---

## 1. `fedBuild-manual.md` (1056 → 685) — highest risk, confirmed

### Rank 1 — `iconSizes` / `actionSizes` / `motion` are gone entirely. **WORTH RESTORING.**

The single sharpest loss in the whole set. Backup §3:

> ### Icon sizes, action sizes and motion are NOT theme tokens
> These collide with Chakra scales too (`theme.sizes.lg` is 32rem and backs `w`/`h`/`boxSize` everywhere), so they're **imported as constants** instead:
> ```tsx
> import { iconSizes, actionSizes, motion } from 'app/theme/foundation';
> <Icon boxSize={iconSizes.lg} />                    // 20px
> <Button height={actionSizes.height.lg} />          // 52px
> ```
> `iconSizes` — `lg` 20 · `md` 16 · `sm` 12
> `actionSizes` — `height.{lg:52, md:40}` · `paddingX.{lg:32, md:20}` · `gap:16`
> `motion` — `duration.{fast:200ms, default:300ms, slow:500ms}` · `easing.{standard, slides, fades}`
> ⚠️ **Motion values are PROVISIONAL** and pending designer sign-off.

Across all three new files, `iconSizes`/`actionSizes` appear **once**, in a list of things `zimmTokens.ts` imports (`uiBuild-knowledge.md:33`). `motion` appears nowhere as guidance. The PROVISIONAL warning is gone.

**Verified still current:** `sizes.ts` exists with exactly those values, and its own header comment says *"Import these constants directly instead — `<Icon boxSize={iconSizes.lg} />`"*. `motion.ts` still carries `PROVISIONAL: Motion design is pending formal sign-off`.

Why this costs the most: the new docs spend three separate passages warning that a bare key on `boxSize`/`width` is an 8×–112× blow-up, and that a raw px literal is an `audit:tokens` violation — **then never say what the correct answer is.** A developer sizing an icon now has both wrong answers documented and the right one deleted.

### Rank 2 — the Storybook `ignore-loader` empty-icon fact. **WORTH RESTORING.**

> Base-template SVGs are `ignore-loader`ed in `.storybook/main.js`, mirroring the browser build. Any icon sourced from `@salesforce/retail-react-app` therefore renders as an **empty box** in Storybook while rendering correctly in the app. Twelve of `ZimmIcon`'s types are currently in that state. Our own icons in `zimm.tsx` are unaffected — so an icon that appears blank in Storybook is usually a sourcing signal, not a broken glyph.

Zero hits for `ignore-loader` or `empty box` in the new set. Pure debugging-hours loss, and it pairs with the `ZimmIcon`-throws-under-Vitest note that *was* kept (`uiBuild` §10) — the two are the same root cause and only half survived.

### Rank 3 — the 22 `textStyle` names. **WORTH RESTORING.**

New docs say only *"All 22 Handover text styles are registered"* (`fedBuild-manual.md:167`). The enumerated list — `heading1Strong heading1 heading2 heading3 · body1Strong body1 body2Strong body2 · mobileBody1Strong mobileBody1 mobileBody2 · label caption · linkLg linkSm · button buttonSm · productNames price · navigation · footer · serif` — is gone from all three.

**Verified:** `typography.ts` still defines exactly those 22 keys. `textStyle` is the mandatory first rung of the hierarchy in all three new docs; the list of legal values for that rung now exists nowhere in the doc set.

### Rank 4 — three `extendTheme` merge mechanics. **WORTH RESTORING.**

Three distinct facts, all gone:

**(a) The `parts` rule:**
> Always declare your own `parts` array. A recipe with no `parts` inherits the base's list, so any Zimmermann part you add is undeclared.

**(b) The reordering mechanism** (the subtle half of the merge trap):
> A key that already exists in the base keeps the *base's* position in the merged object; a key you add that the base lacks is appended **last**.

Both new docs state *that* `extendTheme` merges and *that* shorthand-after-longhand resets — but neither says the merge is what **reorders** them. `uiBuild` §2 splits these into separate numbered items (1 and 4) with no link, so the causal chain that made the footer's `subscribeHeading` gap collapse is no longer derivable.

**(c) The inspection command:**
> ```js
> theme.components.Header.baseStyle   // merged — what actually applies
> ```

### Rank 5 — `test-storybook` / `build-storybook` commands. **WORTH RESTORING.**

`fedBuild` §9 says *"Storybook interaction tests are a separate command against a *built* Storybook"* — and never names it. Backup: `npm run build-storybook && npx test-storybook`. ## 2. `uiBuild-knowledge.md` (456 → 690) — grew, but §6 got worse

This file gained substantially (§8 CMS tiers, §11 signposts). Its losses are concentrated and one is actively harmful.

### The §6 rewrite is a degradation, not a compression. **WORTH RESTORING — all six.**

Backup §6 was six mechanisms with mechanisms and fixes. New §6 is headed *"Six mechanisms, each with its fix"* and four of the six state no mechanism and no fix. Four are **materially different claims**:

| # | Backup | New | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | "A wrapped element takes **available width, not its longest line**. `width: min-content` resolves to the widest unbreakable run." | "a wrapper **shrinks to content** unless told otherwise" | **Opposite claim.** `min-content` gone (zero hits) |
| 2 | "`minHeight` plus `align-items: center` **loses leading when content wraps**… Derive height from `lineHeight` plus padding instead." | "reserves space without collapsing when empty" | **Bug turned into a feature.** The fix is gone |
| 3 | "a block `<li>` wrapping an `inline-flex` `<a>` adds roughly 1.5-2px per row… **Fix with `display: flex` on the `<li>`**" | "use **`display: block`** or set `lineHeight` explicitly" | **The new fix is the bug.** See below |
| 4 | "If the design nests a group inside a stack with no gap, do not reproduce it as a sibling in a gapped flex container… **Give the gap to the heading (`marginBottom`)** rather than the column." | "the parent owns the gap, **never the child's margin**" | **Direct inversion of the prescription** |

**#3 verified against the shipped code.** `overrides/app/components/footer/footerNavColumn/footerNavColumn.css.ts:63-69`:

> ```
> // display:flex, not the default list-item. ZimmNavItem renders an inline-flex <a> of
> // exactly 24px, but a block-level <li> wraps it in a line box whose 24px strut adds
> // descender space below the baseline — measured 25.5px against the anchor's 24px. That
> // 1.5px leaked once per row … making the links column 9px taller than Figma's 158px.
> // Making the <li> a flex container removes the line box entirely
> listItem: { listStyle: 'none', display: 'flex' },
> ```

`display: block` is precisely the state that caused the defect. The new doc prescribes it as the fix. This is the only place in the audit where the revision would actively reintroduce a shipped bug.

### `textStyle` can never emit a `var()` — and the 85% consequence. **WORTH RESTORING.**

> `zimmTokens.ts` imports *from* `typography.ts`, so the reverse would be a circular import. `textStyle` therefore always expands to resolved literals at build time. **This is correct behaviour, not a defect** — and it means roughly **85% of what an emitted-CSS audit flags as "raw literals" is `textStyle` working as designed.**

Zero hits for `circular import` or the 85% figure. This is the fact that stops the next `audit:tokens` run from being misread — and `audit:tokens` is now cited in five places across the new set with an open "triage 19 findings" action.

Gone from `uiBuild`, and its worked table gone from `fedLead` Play 5b. The gate:

> 1. **Same unit?** rem and px are not interchangeable… 2. **Same semantic scale?**… 3. **Is the target permitted?** `--zimm-scale-NNN` numeric aliases are class-only.

**2. `fedBuild` §3 marks the same construct ❌ and ✅ eleven lines apart.**

Line 205: `padding: 'xl',   // ✅ reads theme.space.xl`

## 6. Voice / register drift

Measured markers (`^\`\`\`` fences, `^|` table rows, standalone "you"):

| | fences | table rows | "you" |
|---|---|---|---|
| fedBuild backup → new | 56 → **28** | 99 → **35** | 86 → **21** |
| fedLead backup → new | 6 → 2 | 134 → **46** | 23 → 20 |
| uiBuild backup → new | 10 → 16 | 10 → 25 | 7 → 4 |

**`fedBuild-manual.md` — the clearest drift.** Its established register was instructional second-person and code-heavy. The doc shrank 35% but lost **76% of its second-person address** and **half its code blocks**. It has migrated toward `uiBuild`'s declarative reference register. Specific sections that break it:

- **§10 "Responding to a CodeRabbit review"**, and especially **"What the declines on PR #59 established"** — seven bullets of governance precedent (*"Being Tier 1 is not by itself disqualifying"*, *"Declining on mootness is the weak position"*). This is case-law reasoning aimed at a lead, not procedure aimed at a builder. It belongs to `fedLead`'s subject matter and register.
- **§3's two `[CORRECTED]` blocks** — the backup fedBuild had zero. `[CORRECTED]` is `uiBuild`'s declared convention (its header defines it). Importing it puts documentation-maintenance meta-commentary ("An earlier revision of this manual taught…") inside a how-to, and it's now the second-longest passage in §3.
- **§9's PR-#59 forensic narrative** — same shape.

**`fedLead-playbook.md` — table-first register thinned by two-thirds** while the doc shrank only 14%. Specific breaks:

- **§3 "Principles" and §4 "Working with AI tooling"** are prose-and-aphorism, second-person, coaching register — *"An assistant that agrees with you is worth nothing."* *"Polishing is procrastination."* *"Define done, or nothing stops."* This is the retired playbook's essayistic voice imported largely intact, and it sits ~120 lines before a governance section that is almost pure table. §4's audit-loop passage is also first-person-plural confessional (*"came from **reading code we'd just written**"*), which appears nowhere else in the document.
- **"Integration and vendor boundaries"** — bullet-prose with narrative headers (*"Four things that will bite"*, *"Two integrations degrade in ways QA will file as defects"*). Discursive where the document's habit is a table.

**`uiBuild-knowledge.md` — largely faithful** (near-impersonal, bold-lead-in + declarative, "you" only 4×). Three localised breaks:

- **§4** switches to second-person imperative throughout (*"a base-path import… silently renders the unstyled base version… the story looks like it's exercising **your** override and isn't"*; *"When importing a component that already has an override, **use** a relative path"*). The backup's equivalent was impersonal: *"Inside an override, import a sibling override by relative path."*
- **§7's** *"The three-tier policy — **the most reusable decision** in the footer build"* and *"The per-item case is **the carefully argued one**"* — evaluative editorialising in a document whose stated posture is measured-not-inherited.
- **§6** — a structural break rather than tonal: the header promises *"Six mechanisms, each with its fix"* and delivers six unelaborated one-liners, four of which contain neither. It reads as an unfinished compression of the backup's section, and it's where the substantive errors are.

## Summary — top ten by cost-if-needed

1. `iconSizes` / `actionSizes` / `motion` — the docs now forbid both wrong answers and delete the right one *(fedBuild)*
2. `uiBuild` §6 item 3 prescribes `display: block`, which is the bug the shipped code fixes with `display: flex` — the only change that would reintroduce a defect
3. Storybook `ignore-loader` empty-icon fact — pure debugging hours *(fedBuild)*
4. The 22 `textStyle` names — the mandatory first rung has no legal-values list *(fedBuild)*
5. `CardBaseline` cited as a live reference; verified nonexistent — a deleted warning replaced by a false pointer *(uiBuild §4)*
6. The `parts` array rule + the merge-reordering mechanism + the merged-recipe inspection line *(fedBuild)*
7. `test-storybook` / `build-storybook` / `npm run storybook` command names *(fedBuild)*
8. semgrep XSS + payment-credential rules — the only security gates in the review layer *(fedBuild + fedLead)*
9. The override-first *positive* case (`product-view`'s `addToCart`, resolver propagation) — estimation-relevant, and `product-view` is now live *(fedBuild + fedLead)*
10. `fedLead` Play 8's open-items register — six live, decision-blocking product questions replaced wholesale by infra items

The `fedBuild` prediction held: it lost the most, and the losses are disproportionately *reference material* (token values, command names, enumerated scales) rather than reasoning — the reasoning mostly survived, sometimes twice. `uiBuild` grew but its §6 compression introduced the only outright-wrong content in the revision. `fedLead` traded a product/design/refinement register for an infra/governance one; the new material is strong, but the trade was not additive.
